articles.title: From 50p gold hot pants to Paul Smith suits: how Kylie Minogue became one of pop’s ultimate chameleons
articles.summary: The star’s rise from Ramsay Street to global superstar is the subject of a new book. It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shock. On 20 December 1989, Kylie Minogue first harnessed the power of fashion.
body: Before then, there’d been her Neighbours character Charlene’s peak-80s silk taffeta and lace wedding dress, and Kylie the pop star on the cover of her first album, in 1988, wearing a topless hat showing off cascading curls. But that had been fashion forced on her, at a time when she had no say in her image.

From that moment, Kylie, or the public-facing version at least, took control. She used fashion as a reflection of her desire and need to evolve. Forever the pop chameleon, she anchored each new era via deliberate fashion choices that communicated where she was at in her life and career. As Jean Paul Gaultier wrote in the foreword to her 2012 photo-book Kylie/Fashion: “You change, you transform yourself, you adapt with the evolution of times, fashions, desires … and still stay yourself.”

It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shock.

articles.title: Remake review – Ross McElwee’s magnificent and moving tribute to a tragic loss and the art it inspired
articles.summary: Sherman’s March director McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making art. This new film from revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee is an extraordinary work, arguably his most audacious use yet of autobiographical material while at the…
body: On that very simplest level, Remake starts out as a documentation of how Hollywood got in touch with McElwee and told him they wanted to make a fictionalised remake of his best-known film, Sherman’s March. Made in 1985 with a one-man crew (McElwee himself), Sherman’s March recorded the McElwee’s trip back to South Carolina where he grew up; there he films his family, old friends, and himself as he continually fails to establish romantic relationships with various women, all of it lavishly slathered with his own warm, softly southern-accented voiceover.

Remake slowly reveals what it was that led to Adrian’s death – not in order to create any kind of salacious mystery, but because it only makes sense, as much as something so senseless ever will, after we’ve got to know Adrian better: his aspirations and his troubles, a bipolar diagnosis, the deep wells of self-doubt that are not unlike his father’s. The end result is a profoundly moving work, one that will resonate with anyone who is a parent or close to a troubled kid, but one that has so much more about the making of art, its joys and its dishonesties. It lingers in the mind long after the tears have dried.
points: Sherman’s March director McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making art.

articles.title: Byron Bay’s ‘daggier neighbour’ named in Lonely Planet’s 2027 Best in Travel list
articles.summary: The Tweed region is easily as beautiful as nearby Byron, but without the glamour and crowds. For locals, the biggest drawcard is the community. Locals in the Tweed region already knew we were a bit special, obviously. The sheer beauty of the place routinely stops you in your tracks.
body: Now those who came here to escape the world may find it is coming to them.
“Bloody hell,” says a fellow resident Sarah Killington, whose verandah overlooks the wide, flat Tweed Valley. “We don’t want to turn into another Gold Coast.”

Jessica Lockhard, Lonely Planet’s destination editor for Oceania, says that the Tweed was chosen because: “What we’re really looking for is places that feel less crowded, that are offering a deeper and more meaningful experience, or are really inviting travellers to slow down.” We can definitely do slow.

Tweed Shire is Byron Shire adjacent, easily as beautiful but without the glamour. There are fewer “healers” and drum circles, less tourist overcrowding and recently arrived wealth. We are traditionally the poorer, daggier neighbour. And we like it that way. A place that people usually drive past on their way from the Gold Coast to Byron Bay. You can almost feel the atmosphere change when you enter Byron.

articles.title: A moment that changed me: my brother gave me an unexpected gift – and a whole new life at sea
articles.summary: The water was my childhood playground but, as I grew up, my health left me landbound. Then my brother found a way to launch me back into the waves... My brother and I grew up surfing at Porthcawl in south Wales.
body: I was in my teens when I started to develop chronic illnesses, including endometriosis. At first, I was still able to surf – I just needed to rest afterwards. Then, in my early 20s, I developed further chronic conditions, including a connective tissue disorder that affected my joints and muscle strength. I could stand just for a few seconds and was able to walk only a few metres. At 23, an acute infection led to complications, including the loss of the use of my legs. Later, my stomach became paralysed; I’m now fed via a tube that runs down my oesophagus, through my stomach and into my intestines.

When I was 24, one year after becoming a full-time wheelchair user, my brother, Leon, gave me an unexpected birthday gift: a battered, pink and yellow surfboard to which he had fitted shower handles either side of where my chest would rest. He was training as an adaptive surf coach, he explained, so that he could teach me.

At a time when every day seemed like a riptide threatening to drag me into another hospital admission, the new surfboard felt like an ambitious gift. But it also sparked a desire to adapt and take risks again. It was crying out for the sea.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Behind the Scenes at Vogue World 2026: Milano
articles.summary: Mere minutes after Vogue World: Milano wrapped, Chloe, Nicole, and Vogue Italia’s Francesca Ragazzi gathered in a nearby ristorante to recap the evening’s goings on.
body: After taking in the Prada and Diesel shows that kicked off Milan Fashion Week, they were off to the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II for Vogue World, and its sprawling celebration of Italian design across time. The clothes, the models, the performances—a night honoring the best of Italian fashion and craftsmanship simply had to be over the top.

The group then identified their highlights from the show. For Nicole, seeing the designers sitting in the front row was a standout moment. “It was really fun to watch everyone watching their designs in the show,” she said.

Chloe was a big fan of the songs and dancing, in particular the young choristers from La Scala, Alicia Keys, and Roberto Bolle ’s performance. And Fran couldn’t help but express her gratitude to the many teams of people who made the event happen: “I’ve never seen such harmony and teamwork.”

articles.title: Simone Ashley Looked Like the Boss at Vogue World Milan 2026
articles.summary: Simone Ashley may have just played the role of Miranda Priestly’s assistant in “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” but when walking the runway at Vogue World: Milano, she looked the part of a boss. Ashley marched down the runway in a custom pinstripe Tod’s suit detailed with a belt displaying her initials.
body: The actress (and, now, singer, after she released her debut EP, Songs I Wrote in New York, earlier this year) was part of Vogue World: Milan’s third act, which mimicked a typical day in the life at the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, the site of the show.

All of the typical characters who could be seen passing through the historic shopping center on an average day in Milan were present: a mom pushing a baby in a stroller, a woman on her phone, a traveling couple pulling luggage, students gathering, and sciura scurrying. Fellow actresses Madelyn Cline and Laura Harrier, along with the professional skateboarder Keegan Palmer and a number of players from Inter Milan and AC Milan, were also there—what a day at the Galleria!

articles.title: The Best Boxed Stuffing Mix, According to Our Taste Test
articles.summary: We tasted seven popular stuffing mixes from Stove Top, Pepperidge Farm, Trader Joe’s, and more. These three came out on top.
body: Boxed stuffing may not taste exactly like homemade stuffing, but when Thanksgiving prep starts to feel chaotic, a good mix is a shortcut worth taking.

The best boxed stuffing should have the hallmarks of a great homemade version: a soft, fluffy interior, a crisp, bronzed top, and plenty of buttery, savory flavor. We looked for mixes with distinct pieces of bread that absorbed moisture without turning soggy or stodgy, plus enough sage, rosemary, parsley, and other aromatics to make every bite taste like Thanksgiving.

We tested seven popular boxed stuffing mixes to find the ones worth serving. Stove Top Savory Herbs was our favorite overall, Stove Top Traditional Sage was the herbiest, and Pepperidge Farm Herb-Seasoned Classic Stuffing had the freshest flavor and texture.

The clear favorite in our taste test, Stove Top Savory Herbs has an ingredient list similar to our runner up, Stove Top Traditional Sage with one noteworthy difference. Savory Herbs includes MSG, which gives this mix its extra savory boost.
